Overall, this lending model may not allow the big tech lender to compete with traditional banks for the full range of credit services.

Is big tech lending robust to severe economic shocks that disrupt the economy? Interestingly, our sample covers the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, which started in February 2020 and presented an unprecedented shock to every economy in the world. Recent studies by Ben-David et al. (2021) and Bao and Huang (2021) show that fintech lending in both the United States and China during the COVID-19 crisis was not as robust as bank lending. We examine the performance of the big tech lending program after the COVID-19 shock in this section. The COVID-19 crisis is particularly interesting for several reasons. First, to the extent that big tech lending is largely based on behavioral patterns uncovered from historical data, a natural concern is that the COVID-19 shock may have generated a structural break in the economy and 31 One may argue that as the number of the overlapped borrowers is small, the big tech lender may not be so concerned about losing their business. To the extent that the borrowers' characteristics are continuous, the lack of any difference in the big tech lender's strategies to compete for the overlapped borrowers with easily observed access to conventional credit services from Bank X also indicates that the big tech lender does not compete for borrowers with credit access offered by other financial institutions. This set is likely bigger. Furthermore, and perhaps more importantly, the big tech lender may lose even more lending business from not covering the borrowers' financing needs beyond short-term liquidity needs.

thus invalidated model predictions that are based on pre-COVID-19 data. Second, as many small businesses suffered liquidity shocks during the COVID-19 pandemic, it is particularly relevant to examine whether the big tech lending program was able to meet these liquidity needs despite the possible structural changes in the economy. Third, as big tech loans tend to be repaid much quicker than conventional bank loans, a big tech lender might have been able to quickly detect any change in the repayment speed and delinquency rate of its borrowers and consequently adjust its lending strategies in response to the shock. To examine the performance of the big tech loans after the COVID-19 shock, Figure 1, Panel A depicts the monthly loan issuance in millions of RMB of the three types of loans over the sample period. The amount of big tech loan issuance increased steadily over the sample period, while there was a sharp decrease in both online and regular loans for Bank X in February 2020, the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in China. As February 2020 was also the month of the Chinese New Year, Bank X's loan issuance might have shrunk for seasonal reasons related to the national holiday. Nevertheless, big tech lending was stable both before and after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Panel B depicts the average interest rates of each type of loan issued each month over the sample period. The interest rates of all three types of loans were stable during the sample period.

During the months after February 2020, there were steady decreases in the interest rates for all three types of loans, possibly due to the monetary policies implemented by the Chinese government to reduce interest rates and incentivize financial institutions to provide funding to small businesses after the COVID-19 shock. In Table 9, Panel A, we further compare the loan provisions between Hubei province and other provinces during the three months surrounding February 2020. 32 Hubei province was the epicenter of COVID-19 in China, and its economy was the most severely affected by the COVID shock. The comparison between Hubei and other provinces thus provides a useful cross-sectional test of how the three lending programs in our sample reacted to the COVID-19 shock. The variables in the regressions are all at the loan type-geography-month level, where the geography is either Hubei province or all the other provinces combined. The dependent variables include the logarithm of the total loan amount, the logarithm of the number of loans, the fraction of loans issued to new borrowers, and the average interest rate. Bank X's regular loans are the benchmark group in all regressions. The "post-COVID-19 shock" indicator is equal to one for the three months after February 2020, and zero otherwise. The key variable of interest is the triple interaction term between the big tech loan indicator, the Hubei province indicator, and the post-COVID-19 shock indicator.

There is no significant difference in total loan amounts issued by the three lending programs after February in Hubei compared to the other provinces. Yet, column 2 shows a larger number of big tech loans originated in Hubei province after the COVID-19 shock. Interestingly, the last column shows that the interest rate of big tech loans is also lower in Hubei province after the shock. Since the analysis in this table makes no further adjustment to borrower characteristics, we should be cautious in interpreting the findings. Panel B of Table 9 compares the overdue rate of loans issued from January through March 2020, that is, one month before and two months after the COVID-19 shock. We restrict the event window to one month before the COVID-19 shock because big tech loans are repaid quickly and a longer window would lead to many loans having been repaid even before the start of the pandemic. We make the post-event window two months after the shock because the Chinese New Year is celebrated in February, and the number of regular and online loans issued by Bank X is normally low due to the holiday season. 33In all the columns in Panel B, the dependent variable is whether a loan is at least 30 days overdue, and the benchmark group is Bank X's regular loans. 34 The post-COVID-19 shock indicator is equal to one for February and March 2020, and zero for January 2020. The key coefficient of interest is the interaction term between the big tech loan indicator and the post-COVID-19 shock indicator. We do not compare the loan performance between Hubei and other provinces because the number of Bank X's regular and online loans in Hubei is too small to appropriately assess the loan performance. We gradually add controls on loan contract variables, borrower characteristics, and fixed effects into the regression across the specifications.

Across all the specifications, we find a significantly negative coefficient on the key interaction term, suggesting a smaller increase in the overdue rate for big tech loans originated after the COVID-19 shock relative to Bank X's regular loans. Moreover, the magnitude of the estimated coefficient becomes larger from column 2 to column 3 when we control for city × month fixed effects and industry × month fixed effects, suggesting that the smaller increase in the overdue rate of big tech loans originated after the COVID-19 shock is not due to big tech's ability in the selection and timing of local markets, but rather due to its ability in screening borrowers in the same local market in the same time period after the COVID-19 shock. Overall, Table 9 shows that the big tech lending program remained robust to the COVID-19 shock in terms of both the number of loans originated and loan performance. Thus, despite the unprecedented economic stresses brought by the COVID-19 pandemic, the big tech lending program managed to provide financing without incurring greater delinquency risks.

By comparing a sample of big tech business loans made by a pioneer big tech lending program in China with a sample of conventional bank loans, we characterize several key features of the big tech lending model: big tech loans tend to be smaller with higher interest rates, and borrowers tend to repay far before maturity and borrow more frequently. These patterns remain the same for big tech loans made to borrowers with access to bank credit. These sharp patterns suggest that the lender structures its big tech loans to serve the short-term liquidity needs rather than the long-term financing needs of the borrowers in its ecosystem. Interestingly, high interest rates provide an advantageous selection mechanism to select borrowers with short-term liquidity needs, which is in addition to the lender's screening and monitoring capacities facilitated by its technology and ecosystem. This big tech lending model reflects the lender's restrained advantages in providing credit to borrowers in its ecosystem that are underserved by traditional banks, without experiencing more-severe adverse selection or incurring greater risks than banks even during the COVID-19 crisis. This lending model, by design, does not compete with banks to offer a full spectrum of credit services to cover the borrowers' financing needs beyond short-term liquidity needs. Panel A.
